title: Coulomb blockade in microscopic material defects as a source of decoherence and noise in solid-state quantum circuits
authors: R. Banerjee, L. P. Lindoy, M. Hegedus, A. Hutcheson, T. Hawkins, E. Daghigh-Ahmadi, S. Samaddar, T. Barker, J. P. Goff, A. Ya. Tzalenchuk, I. Rungger, S. E. de Graaf
abstract: A critical limitation of solid-state quantum devices arises from the materials from which they are fabricated: uncontrolled surfaces, interfaces, and structural imperfections introduce numerous sources of loss and decoherence. Despite extensive efforts, linking these decoherence mechanisms to their microscopic material origins -- essential for developing effective mitigation strategies -- remains an outstanding challenge that has slowed coherence improvements. Here, using scanning gate microscopy on live superconducting circuits we identify a previously unrecognised decoherence mechanism originating from Coulomb blockade and microwave-driven charge tunnelling in metallic grains. Such grains are ubiquitous in thin-film devices fabricated by standard lithography processes. By characterising multiple defects across different devices, we find such defects to be as common and as debilitating to device performance as two-level system (TLS) defects, while originating from a fundamentally different physical mechanism. Importantly, conventional characterisation techniques would misattribute this loss to other, microwave power-independent processes. Our observations thus reveal a widespread source of decoherence in superconducting circuits, challenging the prevailing paradigm that coherence lifetimes are primarily limited by TLS defects. Eliminating metallic grains during fabrication provides a clear and practical route to suppress this mechanism, offering a pathway towards improved coherence and reduced noise in microwave-based solid-state quantum devices.
summary: The authors report discovering a significant source of decoherence in superconducting quantum circuits caused by Coulomb blockade effects within microscopic metallic grains. Using scanning gate microscopy, they distinguish this mechanism from standard TLS defects through unique spectroscopic signatures. Eliminating these grains during fabrication is proposed as a practical method to improve qubit coherence times.
main_problem: Identifying intrinsic decoherence sources in solid-state quantum circuits that are distinct from previously understood mechanisms like Two-Level System (TLS) defects.
main_result: A novel, widespread decoherence mechanism originating from Coulomb blockade and charge tunneling in ubiquitous metallic grains was identified, challenging the TLS-centric view of coherence limitation.
method: The study combines scanning gate microscopy on live superconducting circuits with theoretical modeling using an Anderson–Holstein-type impurity model to characterize defect dynamics.
model_or_system: The system involves a metallic grain (acting as an 'electron box') tunnel-coupled to the superconducting circuit reservoir, whose charging energy dictates its discrete charge states. The dynamics are analyzed via microwave transmission spectroscopy ($S_{21}$).
key_observables: $S_{21}$ microwave transmission response vs. tip voltage; periodic peaks in $S_{21}$ contours (concentric rings); measurable loss rate ($\kappa$) and frequency shift ($\delta f$).
important_parameters: Charging energy ($E_c$); tunneling coupling strength ($\Gamma$); operating temperature/power regimes; grain size (estimated 10–30 nm).
main_assumptions: Conventional characterization techniques might misattribute this loss to other, microwave power-independent processes; the analysis relies on distinguishing the Sisyphus response from TLS saturation.
figures_summary: Figures show setup schematics and equivalent circuits. Key results include $S_{21}$ contours showing concentric rings (Fig. 1d) and periodic voltage/power dependence in loss rate and frequency shift, which are distinct from power-saturating TLS features.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by first establishing the experimental platform (SGM on superconducting circuits), developing a theoretical model for charge tunneling defects, presenting key diagnostic measurements (concentric rings, periodic response), and concluding with practical implications for device fabrication.
why_interesting: This work provides a concrete example of how localized, non-equilibrium charge dynamics (Coulomb blockade) can dominate decoherence in solid-state qubits, offering new physical insights beyond simple tunneling models relevant to open quantum systems.
